231.t: George Gershwin chooses him for Sportin' Life
231.s: Gershwin went through his manager after seeing him perform repeatedly and chose him for Sportin' Life in Porgy and Bess, a first step beyond his act.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: world of entertainment. He caught me out at one of the theaters some place. He had to catch me. He see me more than one time.

231.t: Smallens tries to throw him out at dress rehearsal
231.s: Conductor Alexander Smallens threatens to throw him out for missing a downbeat; Gershwin calls him a black Toscanini and Bubbles teases Smallens into calm.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: It was in 1935 when I was chosen by the immortal George Gershwin to do the character of Sportin' Life in his new folk opera "Porgy and Bess," at the Alvin Theater in New York City in 1935 and we were to rehearse in different places, the show before and the show going on, naturally, as you might…

231.t: Opening night: missing his entrance and leaping down four flights
231.s: After the crap game scene he was upstairs when the stage manager forgot to call him, and Helen Dowdy yelled that he was on; he jumped four flights.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: However, we do the song, I get the downbeat, I think it was on "Ain't Necessarily So," that this downbeat was given and I didn't take it on time. And from then on we did that, the rehearsal come down great. And after rehearsal, the night of rehearsal, the next day was the opening. And on the…

231.t: Coming in late on the happy dust scene with Bess
231.s: He listens to the music to find his place, talks his way to his song and offers Bess the happy dust, which she refuses.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: And I got down on the stage, you could hear a pin fall, only the music you could hear going. Nobody down there saying you go in here, you go in there, here's where you go in. It wasn't that, I had to go in what I heard going on. So I heard the music and I could tell by the sound of the music where…

231.t: The open fly and the boat-to-New York song
231.s: Told his fly was open, he turns sideways to sing There's a Boat That's Leaving Soon for New York to Bess, and sings its lyrics.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: "All right, I leave it here Maybe you change your mind . . ." and the music plays and I make a turn and turn around and back up and go off.

231.t: The picnic scene: urging Bess to go to New York
231.s: He recounts the next scene where Maria sends Bess to the picnic and he sings Picnics is all right for small town people.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: away, nigger." Then I say, "All right, I'll leave you here" Then I kiss the happy dust in the little package and I put it on the stoop. I say, "All right, I'll leave you here Maybe you'll change your mind" And off I go to my turn and the music is playing and it finishes the song and off I go. And…

231.t: George Gershwin and the production team
231.s: Gershwin left staging to others; the only conflict was DuBose Heyward wanting the lyrics heard and Gershwin wanting the music.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: The only thing I can tell you about him is he's a fine fella, I didn't have no association only this theater. He was a fine fellow. Him and his brother both. Alexander Smallens wasn't bad, neither was Rubin (inaudible). They were all nice people. I loved to do with them.

231.t: Gershwin rehearsing him privately at home
231.s: Gershwin coached him personally on Ain't Necessarily So and the boat song, since he and Buck could not read music.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: No. No. He don't come to rehearsals. In fact I forgot to tell you the part, in my part of 'It Ain't Necessarily So,' he rehearsed me in his private home. He rehearsed me personally. It is the oldest piano in his house.

231.t: Buck as Bingo and being a vaudevillian in opera
231.s: Buck played an insignificant part, but Bubbles insisted he come along; he says his vaudeville background fitted Sportin' Life.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: That's right. That's exactly it. They wanted me without Buck. I said no, because Buck was a character that stood out. Gershwin picked me because I was able to move around and act like a person of the Sportin' Life class, you know. He didn't do a bad pick, 'cause I don't know anybody else

108.t: Conflict with a conductor and winning the principal chair
108.s: A conductor tells him to play without jazz concepts; blind auditions under Jonel Perlea win him principal trumpet.
108.ch: Noble Sissle, Manhattan School and Philadelphia memories
108.q: No. In fact, that was causing me some problems. They had a conductor there. I auditioned a couple of times for the orchestra. He would say, very prissily, “Here in the symphonies, we don’t play with that concept that you fellows play with in jazz orchestras” and so on and so on. One day, I was…

93.t: Bubbles' demand for runner-ups and the Sporting Life role
93.s: Bubbles would ask Green if he had any runner-ups, and Green praises Bubbles' Sporting Life in Porgy and Bess, a favourite of Gershwin.
93.q: inspire anyone that had any kind of entertaining ability, you know, to co-sign what they do, you know, their delivery. Like he played the role -- he introduced the character Sporting Life, you see, and -- in other words, he was being given the catfish role, you know. That's some kind of…
